p: On Thursday, March 4, Maria was on the fourth floor by 6:15, and she still wasn't first. The light was on in the analysts' room. Kiran sat between two monitors with a sleeve of saltines, the way he'd sat most mornings since the sepsis pilot, and the timestamps in his folder said he'd left at one and come back at five.
Ochoa called me last night too, he said before she could ask. Right after you. He said you'd need numbers, and I'd know where they lived.
He thought about it longer than the question deserved. I had the crackers.
At 7:02 an email came in from a man she'd met four times, always across a table with a budget on it.

An email from Glenn Morrow. Subject: One Chart. Maria, Ray says you'll have a business case for the board in thirty days. Glad to help. So neither of us is surprised, here are the three questions I'll ask. One. What does it cost to do nothing? Two. What does it cost if you're wrong? Three. Who owns each benefit after you've moved on to the next thing? I've read a lot of business cases. Most of them answer a fourth question nobody asked, which is how badly everyone wants this. Glenn

She took the legal pad out of her bag, the one from the kitchen drawer. Last night's line was at the top. What does it cost to keep MedaLink? Glenn had asked it first, in politer words. She wrote his other two under it and drew a box around all three.
The board met Friday, April 2. That gave her four weeks to price eighteen months of work at three hospitals she'd spent the winter learning, and to do it without rounding anything up.
On her way out she put a hand on the back of Kiran's chair. Lunch today. A real one. Sure, he said. He didn't.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: what it costs, and what it buys.
Where you are in the life cycle.

Sunday morning at the Greeley diner, Ochoa drew a line across the top of the legal pad and put six tick marks on it. Everybody wants to start at the fourth mark, he said. That's the one where you get to build things.

The systems development life cycle, SDLC, is the path every system takes. Planning decides whether to do it at all, and why. The business case lives here. Analysis finds out what people actually need. Design decides how the system will meet those needs. Build and test makes it and proves it. Implementation puts it in front of users. Maintenance and support run it until it's retired, which starts the cycle over. Waterfall runs the phases in order. Agile and iterative methods loop through them in small pieces. Either way, skipping a phase doesn't skip its work. It moves the work later, where it costs more.

How the exam asks it. Questions describe an activity and ask which phase it belongs to, or what comes first. Funding and the business case come before requirements, and requirements come before design.
What they need, and what's missing.

Needs analysis asks the people doing the work what they require. Gap analysis compares the current state with the future state and lists what's missing between them. Requirements turn each gap into something you can test. "Discharge should be easy" isn't a requirement. "A routine discharge takes 41 clicks or fewer, measured in test" is.

Draw it before you write it. A current state process map shows how the work is done today, workarounds included. A future state map shows how it'll be done after. Swimlanes give each role its own row, so the handoffs show up where the lanes cross. Flowcharts use diamonds for decisions. That butcher paper from Laramie is the most expensive document you own, Ochoa said. It took ten years of workarounds to make.

How the exam asks it. For what an analyst should do first, pick the answer that involves the people who do the work and documents the current state before designing the future one. A good requirement is specific and measurable.
Fix it now, or fix it with the project.

Not every problem should wait for a big project. DMAIC, from Six Sigma, is Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. It fits a complex problem with an unclear cause and plenty of data, and it takes months. PDCA, Plan, Do, Check, Act, is a short cycle: try a small change, measure it, then keep it, adjust it, or drop it. Use it when the change is small, local, and safe to test this week.
How the exam asks it. A small, testable change on one unit points to PDCA. A complex problem with an unclear cause points to DMAIC. Both start from a measured baseline and end by holding the gain.

A business case compares alternatives, and doing nothing is always one of them. Price each one over the same period, against the same criteria. Count every cost: licenses, implementation services, hardware, interfaces, training, the overtime to cover nurses while they're in class, and the internal staff time everybody forgets. That multi-year total is the total cost of ownership.

Know what kind of organization each option has to serve. A critical access hospital is a small rural hospital with no more than 25 inpatient beds, an emergency department open around the clock, and usually no other hospital within 35 miles. Medicare pays it based on its reasonable costs instead of fixed rates, so what it spends, IT included, shapes how it's paid. It isn't a clinic, and an option that treats it like one fails before the math starts.

How the exam asks it. An answer that presents only the preferred option, or compares options over different periods, is wrong. Expect to recognize organization types by their features: beds, services, location, and how they're paid.

Money now is worth more than money later. Net present value discounts each year's net cash flow by (1 r) raised to the year, adds them up, and subtracts the initial cost. The rate r is the organization's cost of capital, and the CFO sets it, not the project. A positive NPV means the project earns more than that rate. Payback period is how long until the cumulative net cash flow covers the initial cost. ROI is total benefits minus total costs, divided by total costs.

Hard benefits are cash you can trace, like a license you stop paying. Soft benefits are real and harder to price, like safer medication passes. Don't turn a soft benefit into dollars with someone else's averages. Report it as a measured outcome with a baseline. Then stress the case. Sensitivity analysis asks what happens to NPV if benefits come in 20 percent low or costs run over. A contingency reserve is money set aside for risks you've named. Glenn doesn't need the case to be big, Ochoa said. He needs to know what happens when it's wrong.

How the exam asks it. Expect to compute NPV, payback, and ROI from a small table. When an answer inflates benefits or hides a financial risk to win approval, it's wrong, even if the project is a good one.

Every benefit needs a baseline measured before the change, and it has to be the right one. If something else moves the measure first, like a new staffing model, the project only gets credit for the gap that's left. Compare like with like. Sicker patients, longer trips, or a different season can explain a difference before the system does.

A benefits realization plan names, for each benefit, the baseline, the target, the measure, the data source, the review dates, and the owner. The owner is the leader whose operation has to deliver it, like a CNO or the revenue cycle director, not IT. Someone checks it after go-live, at six months, a year, and two years.

When you present it, lead with the recommendation and the decision you need. Show the options, the numbers, and the downside on one page, and walk the CFO through it before the meeting so nobody's surprised in front of the board. Ochoa tore the page off. A business case outlives whoever wrote it. Write it for the person who checks.

How the exam asks it. Benefits are owned by the business, measured against a baseline, and reviewed after go-live. Expect analytics items that ask what else could explain a difference. For a board, lead with the recommendation, show risk honestly, and brief key stakeholders first.

By Thursday afternoon Maria knew where Kiran's nights had gone. Since January, between sepsis builds, he'd been building in the Corvane test system: thirty-four order sets for the three Wyoming hospitals, copied from the Corvane hospitals and changed by hand to match MedaLink.
We'll need them anyway, he said. If I keep going, we're three months ahead when the board says yes. Nobody asked. I just didn't want to be behind.
The board hadn't said yes. Nobody had asked the Wyoming nurses what they needed. And Kiran's lunch was still in its bag beside his keyboard.
A. Let him keep building, since the sets will be needed and it puts One Chart ahead.
B. Adopt Corvane's standard implementation method, phases and all, next week.
C. Pause the build, place One Chart in the life cycle, and use his sets as input.
D. Bring in a contractor to help Kiran build, so he isn't doing it alone at night.

Maria draws Ochoa's line on Kiran's whiteboard and puts a dot at the first tick. Planning. The business case decides whether there's a project at all. Then analysis, with Wyoming in the room. Kiran's order sets go in a folder for the requirements sessions, where the Laramie nurses can mark them up. He looks at the dot a long time. So I'm early. You're early and you're tired. Go home at five. He goes home at seven, which is progress.

That's the move. Know where you are in the SDLC. A project in planning needs a decision and a business case, then requirements, then design and build. Early work isn't wasted if it feeds analysis instead of skipping it.

Monday, March 8. Kiran had laid October's inventory beside Corvane's standard build: every job MedaLink did at the three hospitals, line by line, and whether Corvane did it the same way. Most lines matched. Some didn't. For a few, nobody could say.

Walt Hagen called at 7:15, which Renee later said meant he'd been waiting since six. I hear you're writing down what we need, he said. Last time somebody did that, they sent us a survey and built what Fort Collins wanted. What are you doing this time?
A. Send every department a request for its wish list, then compile what comes back.
B. Use Corvane's standard build as the requirements, and have Wyoming adapt to it.
C. Walk the gaps with Wyoming clinicians, and write each one as a testable requirement.
D. Have Corvane write the requirements into the contract, since it knows its system.

Two weeks of sessions, a day at Cheyenne and Laramie and a long video call for Rawlins. Each MedaLink job, how Corvane does it, what's missing, and a line someone can test. They find three gaps nobody knew about: the two state reports, and Laramie's surgery schedule printing to the floor at 5 AM. Walt gets his own line. Forty-one clicks or fewer for a routine discharge. Measured. Write it down. Maria does, in ink. Huh, he says.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Needs analysis and gap analysis compare the current state with the future state, with the people who do the work. Each gap becomes a requirement that's specific and testable, so you can prove later whether you met it.

Wednesday Maria drove to Laramie with the photo Renee had taken in January, printed four feet wide. Five lanes: surgeon, clerk, pharmacy, cabinet, nurse. Three places where a dose went around the scanner.

Renee had saved the same conference room. Jess came on her break, and the pharmacist from downstairs, and Kiran on a laptop propped against the coffee pot again. Somebody had to draw what One Chart would look like on this floor, and the business case needed to know what it would cost to get there.
A. Hang Corvane's standard medication workflow beside it as the future state.
B. Draw the future state with analysts in Fort Collins, then show it to the nurses.
C. Skip the map, since the gap list already covers the medication workflow.
D. Draw the future state with the same nurses, lane for lane beside the old one.

They draw it on a second roll, lane for lane. Two of the three workarounds disappear in the new lanes. The third doesn't. Corvane can scan a liquid only if it has a barcode, and Laramie's pharmacy has no way to print one. That's a label printer, a pharmacy tech's hours, and a line in the business case Maria didn't know she needed. Jess taps the new lane at the top, Cheyenne's pharmacists. So at night somebody actually checks.

Exactly right. Current and future state process maps, drawn with the people who do the work, show what changes, what doesn't, and what the change will need. A gap found on paper is cheaper than one found at go-live.

Friday Gail called from Rawlins. Remote verification was twelve nights old, and she'd been watching her own numbers. Nights are better. Days aren't. My day nurses picked up the Given, no scan habit last spring, and they've kept it. I'm not waiting eighteen months for One Chart to fix my day shift.
Kiran was on the call, and he had an idea ready, as he always did: a full improvement project, Six Sigma style, with a charter and a black belt from the quality department.
A. Help Gail run a small PDCA test on one day shift, measured each week.
B. Charter a full DMAIC project with the quality department, as Kiran suggests.
C. Tell Gail One Chart will fix it, and ask her nurses to hold on until then.
D. Have Kiran remove the Given, no scan button from MedaLink at Rawlins now.

Plan: the charge nurse pulls the Given, no scan list at noon and asks about each one, out loud and kindly. Do: one week on days. Check: the day shift scan rate goes from 70 to 78. Act: keep it, and add evenings. Gail names it the noon list. Maria writes a note on her legal pad for Glenn. Whatever the noon list fixes, One Chart doesn't get credit for.

That's the move. PDCA fits a small, safe change you can test this week: plan it, do it, check the measure, act on what you learned. And once it works, the baseline your business case uses has to include it.

Tuesday, March 16, Glenn Morrow came to Maria's office at eight, after Ochoa had finished with her, and sat in the chair by the window with her draft and a pencil. He was a slight, tidy man who'd been CFO for nine years and read numbers the way Walt read clicks.

Rawlins, he said. Twenty-two beds, and it loses money most years. Four million of this is for a building that averages fourteen patients. Why not put it on Corvane's clinic system, the one the forty clinics use? It's a fraction of the cost.
A. Agree, and plan Rawlins on the clinic system to cut that part of the cost.
B. Explain that Rawlins is a critical access hospital, and what that means for it.
C. Move Rawlins to a second phase, a year after Cheyenne and Laramie go live.
D. Tell Glenn this is a patient safety decision, and cost shouldn't decide it.

Maria gives it to him in order. Twenty-two inpatient beds, some of them swing beds. An emergency room open all night with one doctor, the only one for a hundred miles of I-80. Inpatients need an inpatient record: orders, an eMAR, BCMA. A clinic system has none of that. And Medicare pays Rawlins on its reasonable costs, so part of what One Chart costs there comes back through its cost report. Glenn has stopped writing. My first job was the cost report for a twenty-bed hospital in western Nebraska. He crosses out a line. Ask my reimbursement team for that number. Don't guess it.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Know the type of organization and what it does. A critical access hospital is a small rural inpatient hospital with round-the-clock emergency care and cost-based Medicare payment. It needs an inpatient system, and its payment model belongs in the business case.
Glenn had left one more question in pencil in the margin of page one. Why not pay somebody to keep MedaLink running? Ochoa had asked the same thing in October.

Kiran had prices by Wednesday. A third-party support firm would keep MedaLink patched after its vendor walked away. A smaller EHR company had quoted the three hospitals on their own. And Marcus had sent a count: sixty-four Relay interfaces touched MedaLink, and on every road but standing still, each one would be rebuilt or retired.
A. Include the others too, but price them high, so that One Chart stands out.
B. Price all four over five years, doing nothing too, on the same criteria.
C. Compare One Chart with third-party support, the option Glenn asked about.
D. Present One Chart alone, since it's the only option that gives one record.

Four columns, five years, every cost in each. Doing nothing: $16.0 million, and no patches after June 2028. Third-party support: $22.0 million, and still two records. The smaller vendor: $19.0 million, counting a year of MedaLink overlap, and now three records. One Chart: $17.0 million, plus $1.5 million of MedaLink still running in year one, $18.5 million, and one record. Under each, the same rows: safety, the system plan's one-record goal, risk, and what the nurses give up in the change. Glenn reads it. Doing nothing is the cheapest, and you put it first. It is the cheapest. Until it isn't.

Exactly right. Evaluate alternate solutions side by side: same period, same cost categories, same criteria. Include doing nothing as the baseline. Showing that it's cheaper and still unacceptable makes the case stronger.

Aisha sent the transfer numbers Friday with three exclamation points. Kiran had pulled every 2026 transfer from the three Wyoming hospitals to Greeley and Fort Collins, 2,000 of them. Thirty-eight percent had the same labs or scans repeated within six hours of arrival. For transfers between Corvane hospitals, it was fifteen percent.
Twenty-three points, she wrote. That's the record. The receiving doctor can't see what Wyoming already did, so they do it again. Put it in.
At $2,500 a repeat workup, twenty-three points on 2,000 transfers came to $1.15 million a year.
A. Leave the transfers out of the case, since the data are too messy to trust.
B. Put the full twenty-three points in, since the record gap explains it.
C. Compare like with like, matching diagnosis and the hours since the last draw.
D. Use half the gap, about twelve points, so the number is safely conservative.

Kiran matches them overnight, though Maria didn't ask him to do it overnight. The Wyoming patients were sicker, and most rode two to three hours, long enough that some labs needed repeating anyway. Matched, the gap is ten points. Aisha has two ED doctors read fifty of the repeats, and most of the ten were tests nobody in Greeley could see. Ten points on 2,000 transfers is 200 workups, $500,000 a year. Aisha frowns. Smaller. And Glenn will believe it.

That's the move. Interpreting outcomes means asking what else could explain a difference. Adjust for case mix and timing, check the result with clinicians, and put the number that survives in the case.
Monday morning Kiran sent the Rawlins nights, week by week.

Rawlins BCMA scan compliance, night shift, by week. Percent of night doses scanned. Eight weeks before remote verification started on March 1, then three weeks after. The median of the eight baseline weeks is 62.
Aisha's draft benefit was already in the file. One Chart brings Rawlins scan compliance from 62 percent to 95. Glenn had circled the 62.
A. Drop BCMA from the case, since telepharmacy has already fixed the problem.
B. Credit telepharmacy, let the new level settle, and claim only the gap left.
C. Use 80, this week's number, as the new baseline for the Rawlins nights.
D. Keep 62 as the baseline, since that's where Rawlins was when the case began.

Maria rewrites the line. Rawlins nights rose the week Cheyenne started verifying, and all three weeks since sit above every baseline week. That gain belongs to telepharmacy, and the day shift's belongs to the noon list. The case will use the new level once it holds for six weeks, and One Chart claims only what's left: scans MedaLink can't support, like liquids without barcodes. She sends it to Aisha first. Aisha writes back one word. Fair. Then a second message. Annoyingly.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Read a measure over time against its own baseline, and credit the change to what actually changed. When something else moves the measure first, re-baseline once it's stable and claim only the gap that's left.
Wednesday Aisha forwarded an email with a spreadsheet attached and a note on top.

An email from Brett Talbot. Subject: One Chart ROI. Aisha, here's the Corvane value calculator our customers use for board cases. Plug in your beds and it does the rest. Medication safety alone comes out around $2.4 million a year for three hospitals your size. Most boards like that line.
He's selling, I know, she wrote. But safety is the real reason we're doing this, and right now it's worth zero dollars in your case. Glenn only reads dollars.
With the calculator's line, the NPV went from just under six hundred thousand dollars to about ten million.
A. Include half the calculator's figure, $1.2 million, as a careful middle.
B. Use the calculator's $2.4 million, since safety is why we're doing this.
C. Leave safety out of the case entirely, so that every number in it is hard.
D. Keep NPV to hard dollars, and show safety as measured outcomes instead.

Two parts. On page one, the NPV, built on dollars Cascade can trace. Right under it, a box: what One Chart buys that isn't priced. Scan compliance by hospital, against the new baselines. Medication errors reported. Transfer med lists that arrive complete. Each measured now, each with a target. Aisha stops on the box. It's not dollars. It's patients. He reads those too.

Exactly right. In cost-benefit analysis, keep hard and soft benefits apart. Price only what you can trace. Present the rest as measured outcomes with baselines and owners, so they're visible without inflating the math.

Friday Glenn went through the draft line by line in his own office, with his reimbursement director on speaker and the door closed. He checked the discount rate, his 8 percent. He checked the MedaLink invoices, and the overtime to cover nurses while they trained.

He didn't find anything to change, and that seemed to worry him more than if he had. $586,000 of NPV on twelve million, he said. That's thin. So here's my question two. What does it cost if you're wrong?
A. Show the downside: named risks, the contingency, and a 20 percent miss.
B. Quietly add 10 percent to every cost line, so the project comes in under budget.
C. Add a flat 10 percent contingency, and present the base case on its own.
D. Tell Glenn the estimates are conservative, so the risk is already covered.

Maria shows him three numbers. The $12.0 million already holds a $1.2 million contingency for named risks, like backfill rates and data conversion. If benefits come in 20 percent low, NPV is minus $2.7 million. If the up-front cost runs 15 percent over, minus $1.2 million. And one risk money can't fix: MedaLink support ends in June 2028 whether Cascade is ready or not. Glenn turns the page back and reads it again. It's thin. It's thin and it's true. I can defend that.

That's the move. Financial risk belongs in the open. Name the risks, size a contingency for them, and run sensitivity on the biggest drivers, so decision makers see how the case fails as well as how it succeeds.
Tuesday at 7:30 Ochoa read the draft at his desk with a red pen he didn't use. Then he turned to the page Glenn's third question had built: the benefits.
Five of them, he said. MedaLink costs retired. Denials. Repeat workups on transfer. Scan compliance. Walt's clicks. Who's going to check, in 2029, whether any of them happened?
A. Measure each benefit at go-live, then close the plan with the project.
B. List a target for each, and let the owners set baselines after go-live.
C. Name Maria's team as the owner of all five, since her team runs the project.
D. Give each one a business owner, a baseline, a target, and review dates.

One table. MedaLink costs: Glenn's finance team, against the 2026 invoices, gone by the end of 2028. Denials: the Wyoming revenue cycle director. Repeat workups: the chief medical officers at Greeley and Fort Collins, where the transfers land. Scan compliance: each hospital's CNO, Gail included. Clicks: Walt, who asked for it. Each with its measure and data source, reviewed at six, twelve, and twenty-four months by the board's finance committee. Ochoa caps the pen. Somebody will be in this chair in 2029, he says. Now they'll know who to call.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. A benefits realization plan names each benefit's owner in the business, its baseline, target, measure, data source, and when it's reviewed after go-live. It keeps the case accountable after the project team moves on.
The board met Friday afternoon, April 2, on the sixth floor. One Chart had twelve minutes on the agenda, between the audit report and the pension plan.

Maria had a sixty-page appendix, four weeks of work, and a one-page summary. Glenn had read all of it. Aisha would be in the room. So would eleven board members who'd last heard about Rawlins the night they learned its numbers had been wrong for a year.
A. Brief Glenn and Aisha first, then lead with the ask, on one page, risks shown.
B. Walk the board through all sixty pages quickly, so they see how thorough it is.
C. Open with Brett's calculator slide, since boards respond to big numbers.
D. Ask Ochoa to present it for her, since he's the one the board knows best.

Glenn and Aisha each walked through the page on Wednesday, so nothing in it surprises them, and Glenn says so out loud. Maria starts with the ask: approve One Chart, $12.0 million, go-live in October 2027. Then the four roads, the NPV with its downside, the safety box, and who owns each benefit. She leaves four minutes for questions. A board member asks what happens if it goes badly. Glenn answers before she can. It's on the page. She put it there. I checked.

Exactly right. Present to executives with the recommendation and the decision first, the evidence on one page, and the risks in plain view. Brief the key stakeholders before the meeting so nobody is surprised in front of the board.
The board voted at 4:20. Eleven yes, no abstentions. The chair asked one more question after the vote, and it wasn't about money.
Rawlins, he said. Is it better today than it was in February? Nights are, Maria said. Days are getting there. The rest is what you just bought.

Then the chair turned a page. The board wanted the implementation partner and the integration platform bid out competitively, with a recommendation by summer. Ms. Santos will run that? Ochoa said she would. Nobody had asked her, which she was learning was how it worked.
Glenn walked her to the elevator. Nine years, he said. First business case I didn't have to take apart. He pushed the button. Don't let the bids make a liar of it.

It had been a month of making numbers smaller. Twenty-three points had become ten. Sixty-two percent had become a baseline that wasn't hers to claim. Ten million had stayed in a vendor's spreadsheet. What was left was a case Glenn could defend and the board could check, with a name beside every promise. It was less than she'd hoped for and more than she'd had, and it would still be true in 2029.

She found Kiran in the analysts' room at 6:30, the only light on the floor, already starting a requirements list for the bids. That morning the cafeteria cashier had stopped Maria to ask whether the young man who used to come in every day at 12:15 was all right. She hadn't had an answer.
Go home, she said. After the RFP. There is no RFP. The board voted two hours ago. Then I'm early, he said, and almost smiled.
He stayed. Maria went back to her office, found Monday's page, wrote KIRAN across the top in capitals, and underlined it twice.

Home by nine. Lucia had Maria's laptop open on the kitchen table, a bowl of cereal next to the keyboard, both against house rules. The one-page summary was on the screen. This is the thing? The whole month?
Sixty more pages in the back. Don't drip milk on it.

Lucia scrolled down and back up. Which part's the nurses? Maria leaned over her and put a finger on the box under the NPV, the Rawlins line. Nights, 62, then the arrow. That's one number. That's every nurse in Rawlins at three in the morning, pulling a dose with nobody to call.
Lucia chewed for a while. Did you round it up? Nope. Huh. Okay. Then she took her cereal and went up to bed.

Maria's phone buzzed at 10:05. Brett Talbot. Subject: Congrats!! Two exclamation points this time. Corvane would love to help with the bids, and was she free for dinner next week, his treat. She didn't open it. It would keep until Monday. So would Brett.
